title: Short Stuff: La Lechuza - The Witch Owl
summary: Short Stuff episode on La Lechuza (the Witch Owl), a legendary shapeshifting owl-woman from Texas-Mexico border folklore. Hosts cover her supposed appearance and behavior (crying-baby lure, talons that snatch people by the scalp, a witch's familiar that abducts children), the vengeful-woman origin stories, the claim that a human is secretly possessed by her, and her bullet-proof reputation. They discuss likely origins as a folk tale used to keep children in line, a possible pre-Columbian Mesoamerican root that Spanish Catholic missionaries/colonizers recast as demonic, and pop culture appearances including a horror film, a Relámpago comic villain by Margarito Garza, and the song "El Paraguas Gigante de Robstown" tied to 1975-76 sightings in Robstown, Texas. The episode ends with a modern reading of La Lechuza as an avenger for abused women and children, and a brief Halloween decorations tangent.
topics: El Paraguas Gigante de Robstown song
folk tales used to discipline children

segments.title: Welcome and Spooky Month kickoff
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short stuff and the hosts announce they are starting a Halloween-themed month, previewing La Lechuza, an owl-woman legend from the Texas-Mexico border.

segments.title: Description of La Lechuza and her crying-baby lure
segments.summary: The hosts describe La Lechuza as a large owl with a woman's face and wingspan, and recount a version where she mimics a crying baby to lure people, then snatches them with her talons.

segments.title: Omens and the vengeful woman origin
segments.summary: Hosts describe the belief that seeing her near a home or dreaming of her portends death or misfortune, and that she is often a woman turned vengeful after cruelty, sometimes a witch's familiar who abducts children.

segments.title: Drunk men, scalp abduction and invulnerability
segments.summary: The hosts describe modern tellings in which she targets drunk men walking home alone, carrying them off by the scalp, and the belief that she cannot be killed by bullets.

segments.title: Human host and unmasking incantation
segments.summary: Josh explains the belief that a human is secretly the owl-woman, unconscious at home while she roams, and a supposed incantation that can reveal the person, though he could not find a source.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Brief break; the hosts tease returning after the break.

segments.title: Name meaning and folk tale as child discipline
segments.summary: Josh notes that la lechuza means owl, and that the legend likely explained disappearances or kept kids well-behaved, similar to European fairy tales.

segments.title: Possible pre-Columbian Mesoamerican origins
segments.summary: Chuck says the origin is hard to trace and may be pre-Columbian Mesoamerican; Josh adds that Mesoamerican gods were often animal-human hybrids and that Spanish Christians recast such deities as demons.

segments.title: Pop culture: horror film, comic, and song
segments.summary: Hosts mention a horror film based on a Latino legend, a Relámpago comic villain created by Margarito Garza, and the song by Los Campeones de Raul Ruiz about Robstown, Texas sightings in 1975 and 1976 that turned out to be a teen-made dummy.

segments.title: Halloween decorations tangent
segments.summary: Chuck wishes he knew a model maker to build a custom La Lechuza yard decoration; Josh notes big-box stores now sell large monsters, and Chuck jokes about listeners building one.

segments.title: Modern avenger reading
segments.summary: Josh says modern versions cast her as an avenger for women and children, targeting men who abuse their wives or children, and Chuck agrees.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the short stuff, and the show's production credit closes the episode.
